title: Nervous system
summary: Neurons, impulses, synapses, the brain, the spinal cord and the autonomic nervous system
cards.0.p: A nerve cell is called a neuron. Its short, branched extensions are called dendrites, and its single long extension is called the axon. A fatty myelin sheath wraps and insulates the axon. The gaps in the sheath are called nodes of Ranvier.
cards.0.key: The cell body holds the nucleus. The branching end of the axon is called the axon terminal. Myelin wraps the axon, not the dendrites.
cards.0.etk.soru: Tap the parts of the neuron.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.0.acik: Dendrites are short, branched extensions that come out of the cell body.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.1.acik: The cell body holds the nucleus and most of the organelles. It runs the neuron's life processes.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.2.acik: The axon is the single long extension that comes out of the cell body.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.3.acik: Myelin is a fatty, insulating sheath that wraps the axon. It speeds up conduction.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.4.acik: A node of Ranvier is a gap in the myelin. The impulse jumps from node to node.
cards.0.etk.noktalar.5.acik: The axon terminal is the branching end of the axon. Its vesicles carry neurotransmitters.
cards.1.h: Types of neurons and glial cells
cards.1.p: A sensory neuron carries a stimulus to the central nervous system. An interneuron processes the information. A motor neuron carries the command to a muscle or gland. Glial cells support the neurons.
cards.1.svg#10: stimulus → receptor → sensory → inter → motor → effector
cards.1.key: Glial cells feed and protect neurons and make the myelin sheath. Mature neurons usually do not divide, but glial cells can.
cards.1.once.soru: Which neuron carries the "contract" command to a muscle in your arm?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: A motor neuron carries the command to a muscle or gland.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: A sensory neuron carries the stimulus to the center.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: An interneuron processes information in the brain and spinal cord.
cards.2.p: In a resting neuron, the outside of the membrane is positive and the inside is negative, with a difference of about −70 mV. The Na⁺-K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ ions out and 2 K⁺ ions in.
cards.2.key: The membrane lets K⁺ through more easily, and K⁺ leaks out. As a result there is more Na⁺ outside and more K⁺ inside. This state is called polarization.
cards.2.once.soru: Does a resting neuron use ATP?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump works nonstop and uses ATP.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The pump also works at rest. The ion flows during a stimulus do not use ATP.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: The pump uses one ATP per cycle.
cards.3.p: When a stimulus passes the threshold, Na⁺ ions enter the cell and the inside of the membrane becomes positive. This is called depolarization. Then K⁺ ions leave and the inside becomes negative again. This is called repolarization. These ion flows do not use ATP.
cards.3.key: The ions pass through channels by diffusion. The pump then moves them back to where they were.
cards.4.p: A stimulus below the threshold does not create an impulse. When the stimulus reaches the threshold, a full-size impulse forms. A stronger stimulus does not make the impulse bigger. It only raises the frequency of impulses. This is called the all-or-none rule.
cards.4.key: This rule applies to a single neuron. A nerve, which is a bundle of neurons, responds to a strong stimulus with more neurons.
cards.5.p: Because myelin is an insulator, ions flow only at the nodes of Ranvier. The impulse jumps from node to node. This speeds up conduction and uses less energy. Conduction is also fast in thick axons.
cards.5.svg#0: unmyelinated axon: point by point, slow
cards.5.svg#2: myelinated axon: jumps from node to node, fast
cards.5.key: In MS, the myelin sheath breaks down. As a result, conduction slows or stops.
cards.6.p: The junction between two cells is called a synapse. The axon terminal releases a neurotransmitter into the gap, and it binds to the next cell. Because vesicles are found only in the axon terminal, transmission is one-way.
cards.6.svg#5: from axon terminal to next cell: one way
cards.6.key: Acetylcholine plays a role in muscle contraction, dopamine in movement and reward, and serotonin in mood. Conduction inside a neuron is electrical, and at most synapses it is chemical.
cards.7.p: The largest part of the brain is the cerebrum, and the corpus callosum connects its two hemispheres. Thinking, memory, speech and voluntary movement are controlled here.
cards.7.svg#14: cortex is gray matter, the right hemisphere controls the left side
cards.7.key: The outer cortex of the cerebrum is gray matter. Vision is handled in the occipital lobe and hearing in the temporal lobe. Voluntary movement starts in the frontal lobe.
cards.7.once.soru: If the left hemisphere of someone's brain is damaged, on which side does paralysis usually appear?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: Each hemisphere usually controls the opposite side of the body.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The nerve pathways cross over. So the left hemisphere controls the right side.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: One hemisphere mostly controls only one side of the body.
cards.8.p: The cerebellum keeps balance and coordinates movement. The thalamus relays every sense except smell to the cerebral cortex. The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst.
cards.8.key: The thalamus and hypothalamus are in the diencephalon. By controlling the pituitary, the hypothalamus links the nervous system to hormones. Damage to the cerebellum does not cause paralysis.
cards.8.once.soru: A person who has been drinking cannot walk straight. Which part is mainly affected?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Balance and movement coordination are controlled by the cerebellum.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: The medulla controls heartbeat and breathing.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger and thirst.
cards.9.p: The brainstem is made of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla, and it connects the brain to the spinal cord. The medulla controls heartbeat, breathing, swallowing and coughing.
cards.9.key: The midbrain controls eye and ear reflexes. The pons links the cerebrum and the cerebellum. Damage to the medulla is directly life-threatening.
cards.9.once.soru: Where is the center that controls heartbeat and breathing?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The heart and breathing centers are in the medulla, in the brainstem.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: The cerebrum controls voluntary actions, but the heartbeat is involuntary.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: The cerebellum keeps balance and coordinates movement.
cards.10.h: The spinal cord and the reflex arc
cards.10.p: The spinal cord is the pathway between the brain and the body, and it is also a reflex center. In a reflex arc, the signal goes from the receptor to a sensory neuron, an interneuron, a motor neuron and the effector, in that order.
cards.10.svg#9: the reflex center is the spinal cord, the brain notices afterward
cards.10.key: In the spinal cord, gray matter is inside and white matter is outside. The knee-jerk reflex has no interneuron. The sensory neuron enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root, and the motor neuron leaves through the ventral root.
cards.11.p: The skull protects the brain, and the vertebrae protect the spinal cord. Three meninges wrap them: the dura mater, the arachnoid and the pia mater. The cerebrospinal fluid between the membranes cushions blows.
cards.11.svg#6: The fluid cushions blows and carries nutrients and waste.
cards.11.key: This fluid lies between the arachnoid and the pia mater. It also carries nutrients and waste and fills the ventricles of the brain.
cards.11.once.soru: What is inflammation of the meninges called?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Inflammation of the meninges is called meningitis.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: In epilepsy, neurons fire in an irregular and excessive way.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Paralysis is the loss of movement in a part of the body.
cards.12.p: The nerves outside the brain and spinal cord make up the peripheral nervous system. The somatic division controls the skeletal muscles. The autonomic division controls the heart, smooth muscles and glands involuntarily.
cards.12.svg#9: autonomic: cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, glands, involuntary
cards.12.key: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The knee-jerk reflex is involuntary, but it is somatic because it uses a skeletal muscle.
cards.12.once.soru: You cannot stop your heartbeat at will. Which division controls the heart?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The autonomic division controls the heart, smooth muscles and glands involuntarily.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: The somatic division controls the skeletal muscles.
cards.13.p: Most internal organs receive nerves from two separate branches, and their effects are opposite. The sympathetic system prepares the body for action. The parasympathetic system brings the body back to normal at rest and supports digestion.
cards.13.key: Your heart racing before an exam is a sympathetic effect. Parasympathetic nerve endings release acetylcholine, and sympathetic endings usually release noradrenaline.
cards.14.p: In Alzheimer's disease, neurons are lost. In Parkinson's disease, the neurons that make dopamine decline. In MS, the myelin sheath breaks down. In epilepsy, neurons fire excessively.
cards.14.svg#13: the substance overstimulates the dopamine reward system
cards.14.svg#14: the brain adapts and needs more for the same effect
cards.14.key: In Alzheimer's, memory weakens. In MS, the immune system attacks myelin. Alcohol, nicotine and drugs affect synapses. In addiction, more and more of the substance is needed for the same effect.
cards.14.once.soru: In Parkinson's disease, the neurons that make which substance decline?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The dopamine-making neurons in the midbrain decline. This causes tremor and slow movement.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: Serotonin is mostly linked to mood.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: Acetylcholine works in muscle contraction. The substance that declines in Parkinson's is dopamine.
cards.15.p:
• In a neuron, the impulse goes from the dendrite to the cell body and then to the axon. Myelin speeds up conduction.
• At rest, the outside of the membrane is positive and the inside is negative. When stimulated, Na⁺ enters first, then K⁺ leaves.
• Transmission at a synapse is chemical and one-way.
• The central nervous system is made of the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral system is divided into somatic and autonomic divisions.
cards.15.svg#7: chemical at a synapse, one way
quiz.0.q: Sort each effect by the autonomic branch that causes it.
quiz.0.e: The sympathetic system prepares the body for action. It speeds up the heart, dilates the pupil, widens the bronchi and reduces saliva. The parasympathetic system does the opposite at rest and speeds up digestion.
quiz.1.q: Match each part of the brain with its job.
quiz.1.e: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, and the medulla controls heartbeat and breathing. The hypothalamus regulates body temperature and water balance, and the thalamus relays the senses to the cerebral cortex. Thinking, memory and speech are controlled by the cerebrum.
quiz.2.q: Put each structure in the division it belongs to.
quiz.2.e: The central nervous system is made of the brain and spinal cord. The brain includes the cerebrum, the cerebellum and the brainstem. The nerves outside these make up the peripheral nervous system. The peripheral system is made of the somatic division and the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches of the autonomic division.
quiz.3.q: On an action potential graph, what happens in the phase where the membrane potential rises quickly from −55 mV to +30 mV?
quiz.3.o.0: Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ enters the cell.
quiz.3.o.1: K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves the cell.
quiz.3.o.2: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump uses ATP to bring Na⁺ in.
quiz.3.o.3: The membrane closes to all ions and the charge rises by itself.
quiz.3.e: The rising phase is depolarization. Na⁺ ions enter by diffusion and the inside of the membrane becomes positive. K⁺ leaves during repolarization, when the potential falls.
quiz.3.y.1: K⁺ leaving causes repolarization and lowers the potential. The fast rise comes from Na⁺ entering.
quiz.3.y.2: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump moves Na⁺ ions out and works slowly. The fast rise comes from Na⁺ channels opening.
quiz.3.y.3: The membrane potential does not change without ion movement. The rise is caused by Na⁺ ions entering through channels.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Follow the impulse, push the membrane to threshold, race a myelinated axon and watch a reflex.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Play the neuron and follow the path the impulse takes.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which path does the impulse follow in a neuron?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: That is the reverse direction. The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body, and the dendrite receives the stimulus.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: Dendrite → cell body → axon → axon terminal
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The stimulus is received at the dendrite and passes through the cell body. Then it travels along the axon and is passed to the next cell at the axon terminal.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Dendrites bring the stimulus to the cell body. The impulse does not go from the cell body to the dendrite.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The inside of a resting membrane is −70 mV compared with the outside. If a stimulus brings the membrane to the −55 mV threshold, an impulse forms. Set the stimulus and press play.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: To raise the membrane from −70 to −55, you need at least +15 mV.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: The threshold was passed. Na⁺ channels opened, Na⁺ ions rushed in and the membrane rose to +30 mV. This is called depolarization. Then K⁺ ions left and the membrane returned to its old state. This is called repolarization. These flows do not use ATP.
A:adimlar.2.metin: You passed the threshold. Now strengthen the stimulus and play with two different values. Then compare the peaks.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: When the stimulus got stronger, what happened to the impulse's peak?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The peak stayed at +30 mV each time. Once the threshold is passed, the impulse is always the same size.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The peak did not shrink. It reached +30 mV in both tries.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: By the all-or-none rule, an impulse forms at full size once the threshold is passed. A strong stimulus does not make the impulse bigger, it makes impulses more often.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Some axons are wrapped in a myelin sheath. The impulse forms again at the nodes of Ranvier between the sheath segments. Press play.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: The impulse reaches the end of which axon first?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The impulse jumps from node to node. In a thick myelinated axon the speed passes 100 m/s, while in an unmyelinated axon it is about 1 m/s.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In an unmyelinated axon, the impulse must form again at every point of the membrane. This slows conduction.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Myelin raises conduction speed a lot. So the impulses do not reach the ends at the same time.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Neurons do not touch each other. Between them is a gap called a synapse. Watch what happens when an impulse reaches the axon terminal.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: How does the impulse cross the synaptic gap?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: At most synapses, electricity does not jump the gap. The transfer is chemical.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Vesicles in the axon terminal release a chemical messenger called a neurotransmitter into the gap.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: The terminal fuses with the next neuron
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Neurons do not fuse with each other, and the gap between them stays.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Your hand touches a hot stove. Play the path of the signal.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Where does the command to pull your hand back come from?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The brain notices the pain later. The hand is pulled back before that.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination. It does not start this reflex.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The interneuron is in the spinal cord, and the signal is passed to the motor neuron before it reaches the brain. That is why the reflex is so fast.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Heartbeat and digestion are controlled involuntarily. The sympathetic system prepares the body for danger, and the parasympathetic system prepares it for rest. Use the switch to go between the two systems.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Which is an effect of the parasympathetic system?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The sympathetic system is what speeds up the heart.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The parasympathetic system is the rest-and-digest system. Through acetylcholine it speeds up digestion and slows the heart.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The sympathetic system is what dilates the pupil. This lets more light into the eye.
A:kapanis.0: The impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body, then along the axon to the axon terminal.
A:kapanis.1: When the membrane passes the −55 mV threshold, Na⁺ enters first and then K⁺ leaves. The impulse follows the all-or-none rule.
A:kapanis.2: In a myelinated axon, the impulse jumps from node to node and travels much faster.
A:kapanis.3: Transmission at a synapse is chemical and one-way.
A:kapanis.4: A reflex is processed in the spinal cord. The brain notices the pain afterward.
